summary: Ammar ibn Yasir (RA) was among the earliest Muslims, from a family that became the first martyrs in Islamic history. His father Yasir, mother Sumayyah, and he himself were subjected to brutal torture by the Quraysh in the early Makkan period. His mother Sumayyah (RA) became Islam's first martyr — killed by Abu Jahl. Ammar is the subject of a famous prophecy of the Prophet ﷺ that he would be killed by a transgressing party, a prediction whose fulfillment at the Battle of Siffin was discussed by Companions and classical scholars alike.
biography:
Ammar ibn Yasir was born around 570 CE in Makkah. His father Yasir ibn Amir was a Yemenite Arab from the Banu Ansi tribe who had come to Makkah in search of a lost brother and settled there as a mawla (client-ally) of the Banu Makhzum clan of Quraysh. His mother Sumayyah bint Khayyat was a freed slave. They were among the most vulnerable members of Makkan society — without tribal protection of their own.

The entire family of Yasir accepted Islam in the earliest period of the Prophet's mission: Yasir, Sumayyah, Ammar, and his brother Abdullah all embraced the faith. Because they had no powerful tribal protector, they were among those most savagely persecuted by the Quraysh, particularly by Abu Jahl ibn Hisham of the Banu Makhzum, who took particular pleasure in tormenting them. They were taken to the scorching desert outside Makkah, laid on hot sand, and tortured. The Prophet ﷺ would pass by and could only say to them: 'Patience, O family of Yasir! Your appointment is Paradise.' (Ibn Hisham, al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah; al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak).

Sumayyah bint Khayyat was killed by Abu Jahl — stabbed with a spear — and became Islam's first martyr. Yasir died shortly after from the effects of torture and became the second martyr. These deaths are among the most sobering episodes in the Seerah, a permanent reminder of what the earliest Muslims sacrificed. Ammar survived, though severely injured.

Under extreme torture, Ammar was compelled to say words of disbelief against his will. When this reached the Prophet ﷺ, he asked Ammar what was in his heart at the time. Ammar said his heart remained full of faith and he had spoken only under coercion. The Prophet ﷺ affirmed him and the relevant verse of the Quran was understood to address his case: 'Whoever disbelieves in Allah after having believed — except one who is compelled while his heart is satisfied with faith — but whoever opens his chest to disbelief, upon them is the wrath of Allah.' (Quran 16:106). Classical scholars including Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim cite this as the context of this verse's revelation, establishing the doctrine of ikrah (coercion) as a recognized excuse in Islamic law.

After the Hijrah to Madinah, Ammar played an active role in the Muslim community. He participated in building the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, carrying double loads of mud brick to speed the construction. The Prophet ﷺ reportedly said to him on that occasion: 'O son of Sumayyah! While the others carry one brick, you carry two. Shall I not give you glad tidings? You will be killed by a transgressing party (al-fi'ah al-baghiyah).' (Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Fitan; numerous chains documented by Ibn Kathir).

Ammar fought at Badr, Uhud, al-Khandaq, Khaybar, and all the major campaigns. He was among the most active participants in the conquest of Egypt under Amr ibn al-As (RA). During the caliphate of Uthman (RA), Ammar was involved in some of the controversies of that period and was among those who traveled to complain of administrative grievances — a role that has been discussed variously by classical historians.

In 36 AH, Ammar joined the forces of Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) against Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan (RA) at the Battle of Siffin. At approximately 90 years of age (his exact age is debated; classical sources put him between 80 and 94), he fought in the battle and was killed. Upon news of his death, the forces of Muawiyah cited it as evidence they must be the transgressing party — because the Prophet ﷺ had said Ammar would be killed by al-fi'ah al-baghiyah (a transgressing faction). The political and theological implications of this narration were debated seriously by subsequent generations. Mainstream Sunni scholarship — including Ibn Kathir, al-Nawawi, and others — holds that the hadith is authentic and sahih, that it was fulfilled at Siffin, and that this characterization applies to Muawiyah's forces as a political-military description without entailing kufr or that those individuals are in the Fire. The fitnah era is treated with the standard Athari approach: all parties had sincere motivations, all were believers, their errors were of ijtihad, and we do not make takfir on any of them.

Ammar is buried at Siffin. He narrated approximately 62 hadith in the major collections.
